flashcards.q: What are the two NEW categories and the one consolidation in OWASP Top 10:2025?
flashcards.a: New: A03 Software Supply Chain Failures (expanded from 2021's A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components) and A10 Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (24 CWEs, fail-open and improper error handling). Consolidation: SSRF, which was its own A10:2021 category, folded into A01 Broken Access Control.

flashcards.q: Injection fell from #3 to #5 in 2025. Why, and does it mean SQLi got less dangerous?
flashcards.a: No. Injection has 62,445 CVEs, the most of any category, and 100% max coverage (everyone tests for it). Its average weighted impact of 4.32 is dragged down because 30,000+ high-frequency/low-impact XSS CVEs share the category with 14,000+ low-frequency/high-impact SQLi CVEs. The rank moved on category composition, not on real-world danger. Avg weighted exploit is still 7.15.

flashcards.q: What is the OWASP Top 10:2025 methodology, in numbers?
flashcards.a: 8th edition. Data on 2.8M applications from 13 named contributors, 589 CWEs analyzed (vs ~400 in 2021, ~30 in 2017), 248 CWEs inside the 10 categories out of 968 in MITRE's dictionary, ~175k CVE-to-CWE records for exploit/impact. Cap of 40 CWEs per category, average 25. Eight categories come from the data; two are voted in by a community survey. CVSS v4 was excluded because it no longer exposes separable exploit and impact subscores.

flashcards.q: What is 'incidence rate' in the OWASP ranking, and why does it ignore frequency?
flashcards.a: The percentage of tested applications with at least one instance of a CWE. Frequency is deliberately ignored because manual testers report a finding once while automated scanners report every instance, so counting instances would measure tooling rather than prevalence.

flashcards.q: What can a bind parameter never replace, and why?
flashcards.a: Identifiers and keywords: table names, column names, ORDER BY direction. The query is parsed and planned at Parse time, before Bind, and the planner needs those tokens to build the plan. Anything you cannot bind must come from a set the server controls (an allowlist), not from a regex.

flashcards.q: What does cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM docs ORDER BY %s', ('created_at',)) actually produce?
flashcards.a: ORDER BY 'created_at' -- sorting by a constant string. It is not injectable and it raises no error; it silently returns an unsorted result set. That silence is why the next commit is usually an f-string. Fix with a server-controlled allowlist plus sql.Identifier().

flashcards.q: Describe what a bind parameter physically does on the wire in PostgreSQL.
flashcards.a: Client sends Parse with SQL text containing $1 placeholders; the server lexes, parses, and plans it once. Client sends Bind with parameter values as a length-prefixed array, then Execute. Parameter bytes never reach the SQL lexer, so no byte sequence can terminate a literal and start a statement. That is why parameterization is a structural guarantee and escaping is best-effort.

flashcards.q: What is second-order SQL injection and why does input sanitization not stop it?
flashcards.a: The payload is stored through a safe parameterized path as literal text, then concatenated into a query later by a different code path (report job, admin tool, migration). Sanitization fails because the value was never malformed on input; it is only dangerous at the second sink. The correct model is parameterize on OUTPUT at every interpreter boundary. Data from your own database is attacker data with higher latency.

flashcards.q: How fast can boolean-blind vs time-based SQLi extract a 60-character bcrypt hash?
flashcards.a: Boolean-blind binary-searches printable ASCII at roughly 7 requests per character: ~420 requests, about 21 seconds at 20 rps. Time-based costs ~7 sleeps x 5s = ~35s per character, so ~35 minutes. That is why time-based is used to CONFIRM the vulnerability and boolean or UNION is used to EXTRACT.

flashcards.q: What does blind SQL injection look like in production logs?
flashcards.a: Time-based: p50 latency on one route quantized to multiples of the sleep interval (pg_sleep(5), SLEEP(5), WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5') with all responses HTTP 200. Boolean-blind: thousands of 200s on one route where the response body alternates between exactly two byte lengths. UNION probing: a run of ORDER BY 1, 2, 3... then UNION SELECT NULL,NULL,... with increasing NULL counts. Out-of-band: DNS queries leaving the DB subnet to a domain you do not own.

flashcards.q: What does CVE-2025-1094 prove about escaping as a SQLi defense?
flashcards.a: PostgreSQL's own escaping APIs (PQescapeLiteral, PQescapeIdentifier, PQescapeString, PQescapeStringConn) failed to neutralize quoting syntax on text that fails UTF-8 validation. CVSS 8.1, fixed 13-Feb-2025 in 17.3/16.7/15.11/14.16/13.19, then the FIX REGRESSED and needed 17.4/16.8/15.12/14.17/13.20 on 20-Feb-2025. Rapid7 found it because exploiting CVE-2024-12356 (BeyondTrust) to RCE required it; that chain reached the US Treasury. If your defense is 'we escape correctly,' your defense is a dependency on someone else's parser edge cases.

flashcards.q: Name the three ways an ORM still gets you SQL injection.
flashcards.a: 1) Escape hatches: .raw(), .extra(), RawSQL(), session.execute(text(f'...')), and Hibernate HQL concatenation which has its own CWE-564. 2) Identifier positions the ORM emits from user input -- CVE-2024-42005 was Django's QuerySet.values()/values_list() on a JSONField using a crafted JSON key unescaped as a COLUMN ALIAS (fixed 4.2.15 / 5.0.8). 3) Dynamic field names passed as **kwargs filters, which is authorization bypass landing in the same incident review.

flashcards.q: How do you handle an IN clause and a LIKE pattern safely?
flashcards.a: IN: never build '(1,2,3)' with str.join. Use '= ANY(%s)' with a real Python list (Postgres), or one placeholder per element. LIKE: the value binds safely, but % and _ in user input become wildcards -- escape them. That is not injection, it is a logic bug and a wildcard-scan DoS (a leading % prevents index use).

flashcards.q: What is the correct SQLi remediation ORDER, and where does a WAF sit?
flashcards.a: 1) Parameterize values, allowlist identifiers, enforce with a CI rule not review. 2) Drop the app DB role to least privilege (converts every finding from 'read everything' to 'read what this service owns'). 3) Suppress DB errors to clients (kills error-based extraction). 4) Authorization at the data-access layer. 5) Pin and scan dependencies. 6) Only then a WAF. A WAF is mitigation, never remediation: comment insertion, case shifting, encodings, and MySQL versioned comments all bypass signatures.

flashcards.q: Why is LLM01 Prompt Injection unsolved, mechanically?
flashcards.a: Every injection defense that works uses TWO transport channels so the interpreter cannot re-parse data as grammar: Parse/Bind for SQL, argv for shells, DOM APIs for HTML. A transformer has ONE token stream -- system prompt, user turn, retrieved chunk, and tool output are all attended to by the same mechanism. There is no Bind message for attention, so there is no way to mark a span as data-not-instructions that the model cannot be argued out of.

flashcards.q: What does EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711) prove about prompt-injection classifiers?
flashcards.a: CVSS 9.3, June 2025, zero-click against Microsoft 365 Copilot: a single crafted email bypassed Microsoft's purpose-built XPIA (Cross-Prompt Injection Attempt) classifier, evaded link redaction using reference-style Markdown, exfiltrated via an auto-fetched image, and routed the callback through a Teams proxy already allowlisted in the CSP. The vendor with the most at stake shipped the classifier and it fell to four chained ordinary web bugs. Classifiers are a layer, not a boundary.

flashcards.q: What was CVE-2026-42208 and what does it teach about the AI stack?
flashcards.a: Pre-authentication SQL injection in LiteLLM, CVSS 9.3, versions 1.81.16 through 1.83.6, patched 1.83.7-stable. The raw Authorization: Bearer header value was concatenated into SQL on the key-verification path, so every LLM route was an entry point and none required credentials. Exploited within 36 hours of GitHub advisory indexing, 17 UNION payloads, targeting LiteLLM_VerificationToken / litellm_credentials / litellm_config. CISA KEV 8-May-2026, FCEB deadline 11-May-2026. Patching is not done: rotate every upstream provider key.

flashcards.q: List the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 (ASI01-ASI10).
flashcards.a: ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack, ASI02 Tool Misuse and Exploitation, ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse, ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution (RCE), ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning, ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication, ASI08 Cascading Failures, ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation, ASI10 Rogue Agents. Published 9-Dec-2025 with 100+ contributors.

flashcards.q: What is the agent security posture, ordered by value per unit of effort?
flashcards.a: Gateway-enforced tool allowlist (not a prompt instruction -- the prompt is the thing under attack); step + token + wall-clock budget; no high-risk tool available in the same turn as a read of untrusted external content; human confirmation on irreversible actions; per-agent identity with short-lived scoped credentials (highest value, slowest to ship); full prompt-to-action traces. If you can only do two in a week: gateway allowlist and the budget.

flashcards.q: How do you ship text-to-SQL without building an RCE service?
flashcards.a: Dedicated read-only DB role scoped to specific views, no base tables; parse the generated SQL and reject anything that is not a single SELECT (no semicolon-separated statements, no filesystem/network functions); a tenant predicate injected by your code, not requested in the prompt; statement_timeout and a row cap; results rendered as escaped text. 'The prompt says only generate SELECT' is a hint to the model, not a control. If the product needs writes, the model proposes a diff and a human approves it.
